title: What this means for energy traders — Sunday, October 25, 2026

sections.overall: The Middle East conflict dominates the week's headlines and connects the markets below. Brent topped $116, a six-month high, while the US pulled non-emergency staff from Saudi Arabia after Houthi strikes (CNBC, CNBC). The same disruption feeds heating oil, diesel and LNG stories. Company-driven trends are quieter: the ledger shows few new corporate actions this week.
sections.CRUDE_OIL: Headlines are driven by geopolitics. Gulf exports have recovered to 24.6mn a day, above the prewar 23.3mn, as ships use alternative routes (Financial Times). That sits beside renewed attacks on shipping and talk of resumed US strikes, so physical flows and risk premium are pulling in different directions. Markets generally treat supply-threat headlines as a risk premium that can fade quickly if diplomacy progresses. Still unclear: whether the reported strike timing after the midterms holds.
sections.NATURAL_GAS: LNG is where company behaviour is visible. Cheniere's long-term agreements with QatarEnergy for 4 million tonnes per annum through 2054 show a major Gulf producer contracting US supply (LNG Prime). Canadian expansion is edging up on the Coastal GasLink phase two contract (LNG Prime). Asian cooperation deals and US capacity announcements are both fading by count. Supply-side notes include Norway's September output at its lowest this year (Rigzone) and UK reliance on imports this winter (Rigzone). A fading count may reflect timing of announcements, not weaker intent.
sections.REFINED_PRODUCTS: Winter exposure is the theme: heating oil costs are reported as more than double in some UK households (BBC News), and the US is drawing on its Northeast heating oil reserve (US DOE). Russian diesel cargoes bound for North America are part of a reported US-Russia deal (The Guardian). Policy-driven supply moves like these are usually read as signs of tightness. The European Commission said there is currently no physical shortage (Rigzone).
sections.CARBON_CREDITS: Durable removal buying is steady, with Google and McKinsey committing to 320,000 credits from a Brazilian project (Carbon Pulse). Policy is the larger variable: EU member states continue ETS reform talks with a deal targeted for December (Carbon Pulse), and final CBAM implementing rules are expected in the last two months of the year (Carbon Pulse).
